analysis.one_liner: Requires agencies to repeal two rules before issuing any new rule that adds costs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died at the end of the 117th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The RED Tape Act would have imposed a "one-in, two-out" rule on federal agencies: before an agency could issue any new rule that creates a financial or administrative burden on businesses or people, it would have to repeal or amend at least two existing burdensome rules, and the new rule's cost could not exceed the cost of the ones repealed. The agency head — not an independent reviewer — would decide and certify those costs. The bill was introduced in April 2021, referred to the Senate Homeland Security committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses subject to federal regulation — the industries whose compliance costs the bill would cap — would gain if it passed. By freezing the total cost of regulation, it would prevent agencies from issuing new workplace, environmental, consumer, and financial protections unless they simultaneously gave up existing ones.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would cap the total cost agencies can impose: every new costly rule must be offset by repealing or amending at least two existing ones, at lower or equal cost [S2][S3].
Agencies would have to weigh whether each old rule has achieved its purpose, become obsolete, overlaps with a new rule, or costs more than its benefits before repealing it [S2][S3].
Agencies would publish semiannual lists of rules they plan to issue or repeal, with cost estimates, in the Unified Agenda [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal rules — for workplace safety, clean air and water, consumer and financial protection, and drug and food safety — would bear the cost if it passed: each new protection could only be issued by trading away two existing ones, and the bill sets no floor on how much protection the public keeps.

drawbacks.text: A hard cost cap would block new rules even when their benefits to the public clearly exceed their costs, since agencies could not exceed the cost of the rules they repeal [S2][S3].

The agency head — not an independent referee — would determine and certify the costs of both new and repealed rules, creating room to classify old rules as 'costly' for repeal and new rules as cheap [S3].
Because the definition of 'covered rule' includes guidance documents, bulletins, and even press releases, routine agency communications could be swept into the offset requirement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real, if diffuse, savings to regulated businesses and add some transparency through published regulatory agendas. But its core mechanism is a cap on regulation, not a reform of it: new protections could only be issued by sacrificing existing ones, with the agency head itself certifying the numbers. An honest supporter would acknowledge that genuinely beneficial rules — where benefits exceed costs — could be blocked under it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced and never moved — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Sullivan introduced the bill on April 20, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S1][S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The action history shows no further action after the referral; the bill never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: agencies kept their authority to issue new rules without offsets, and the rules the bill would have forced them to trade away stayed in place. Businesses hoping for a cap on regulatory costs gained nothing, and the public kept the protections it already had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and people relying on existing rules

for.name: Sen. Dan Sullivan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as its sole sponsor, was responsible for shepherding it; it never advanced past committee referral during his term.

against.name: Sen. Gary Peters
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote; it sat in his committee from referral until the Congress ended.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None joined as cosponsors of the bill, including members of the sponsor's own party.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill, so its partisan shape was never tested — the clearest signal is that all 50 of its sponsor's Republican colleagues declined to cosponsor it, and no Democrat did.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses (manufacturing, energy, finance, and other industries subject to federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would cap the total cost of regulation these industries face, letting them avoid new compliance burdens unless agencies repealed two old rules for each new one. The savings to these industries would come from rules the public no longer gets — new worker, environmental, and consumer protections would be priced out.

Agencies would lose flexibility to issue costly new rules, but the bill would leave the key judgment calls — which rules are 'covered', what they cost, and what to repeal — to the agency head itself, adding process more than external control.
